title: Why Do Cargo Planes Open Their Nose?
description:
The nose of a Boeing seven forty-seven freighter can swing up like a giant mouth, and a forty foot long pallet can roll straight in. That trick is the reason the pilots of every seven forty-seven, even the passenger ones, sit on top of the airplane, in that famous hump. Cargo planes are full of parts like that, doors in strange places, floors that roll, tails that swing open. Today, ten parts of cargo planes, and why each one exists.

Machine Reverse takes apart the machines you see every day and explains, part by part, why each one exists. This video covers 10 parts.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
1:17 1. The nose door
2:43 2. The giant side door
4:00 3. The floor that rolls
5:17 4. The net behind the cockpit
6:48 5. The legs that kneel
8:20 6. The ramp at the back
9:43 7. The tail that swings open
11:01 8. The bubble on top
12:15 9. The walls of the cargo hold
13:39 10. The seat for the loadmaster
14:52 The verdict

Sources:
- 747 hump and nose door from USAF CX-HLS work, SST expectation: ePlane AI, "The original purpose of the Boeing 747" https://www.eplaneai.com/news/the-original-purpose-of-the-boeing-747-beyond-passenger-travel
- 747-400F nose door, 40 ft pallets, 124 t payload, side cargo door, 64 in belly ULDs: Wikipedia, "Boeing 747-400" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_747-400
- 9 g forward restraint for items of mass: 14 CFR 25.561 https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/14/25.561
- National Airlines 102, Bagram 29 April 2013, cargo shift (NTSB): Wikipedia, "National Airlines Flight 102" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Airlines_Flight_102
- An-124 kneeling gear, 120/150 t, 30 t crane, first flight 24 Dec 1982, An-225 destroyed 2022: MigFlug https://migflug.com/afterburner/why-nothing-can-replace-the-antonov-an-124-ruslan/
- Boeing Dreamlifter (747 LCF, swing tail, four built): Wikipedia, "Boeing Dreamlifter" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_Dreamlifter
- Airbus BelugaXL (first flight July 2018, two A350 wings, smile livery vote): Wikipedia, "Airbus BelugaXL" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airbus_BelugaXL
- UPS Airlines Flight 6 (3 Sep 2010, 81,000+ lithium batteries, liner failure, 27 min, aftermath): Wikipedia https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UPS_Airlines_Flight_6
